subject: Georeference xy plot coords to lat/lon given corners

messages.author: 246097adfa09eddd
messages.subject: Georeference xy plot coords to lat/lon given corners
parts:
Dear R Users,

I have trees in a plot mapped onto an xy coordinate system with one of the corners as (0,0). 

If I know the lat/lon of that corner, how can I convert all the tree locations (in x,y from that corner) into lat/lon coordinates?


Test data:
x <- c(240,197,150,485,865)
y <- c(480,465,300,698,288)
x0 <- c(-85.61395) #longitude
y0 <- c(10.83874) #latitude

It seems simple, but after several hours on google...am I missing something obvious?

Thank you,

Catherine

messages.author: 0a5ec6aebf03fb10
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Georeference xy plot coords to lat/lon given corners
parts:
If you don't have the compass bearings or are rusty with trigonometry, this might be an easier approach.  Take it with a grain of salt; it's just a hunch (critical feedback welcome):

Convert x0 and y0 to a projection where the units are meters (eg. UTM using the correct zone for your study area).

Now you can add x and y (assuming those are unit meters) to the projected UTM corner coordinates.  You will end up with your five test points in UTM coordinates.  Project those back to lat/long if that's what you want.  Plot them to make sure they make sense to you.

Scott

messages.author: e22360609d091f39
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Georeference xy plot coords to lat/lon given corners
parts:
Another approach:

You need the lat/lon of at least two points in your grid to be able to translate between grid units and degrees. E.g. 1 unit in the y direction = how many degrees?

Converting your y units to latitude should be straightforward, because the actual length of a degree latitude does not change anywhere on earth.

delta.y = y1 - y2 # grid coordinates
delta.y.lat = y1.lat - y2.lat  # lat coordinates
gridY2lat  <- function(y) y * delta.y.lat/ delta.y
lat2gridY <- function(lat) lat * delta.y / delta.y.lat

converting your x units will be more tricky, because the linear distance of longitude degrees change depending on where you are on earth (because its a sphere). So if you are 100 ft from the north pole 1 degree longitude will be a very small distance, but if you are at the equator it will be around 1 km.

If your area of interest is relatively small (say within a few degrees, not too far from the equator), and you don't need much precision the method above should be fine for calculating x values. 

Otherwise you can use a formula to find the distance of a longitude degree, given latitude:

Longitude = latitude in radians * length of degree at equator
gridX2lat <- function(x,y) {  gridY2lat(y) * pi/180  * lat2gridY(1) } 

Haven't tried this out, but hopefully helpful. Also since this is not really an R question, there are probably some spatial groups at davis that could help out as well.

Good suggestion, Steve.  UC Davis has a geospatial list-serv: https://spatial.ucdavis.edu/resources/

I should have also stated that I was assuming your y-axis was already oriented north-south and x-axis east-west.  Assuming you are doing these operations in R, I found this overview of coordinate systems to be very helpful a few years ago.  It won't solve your problem, but it may help you get 'oriented':  https://www.nceas.ucsb.edu/~frazier/RSpatialGuides/OverviewCoordinateReferenceSystems.pdf
